what.text: Humanin is a small peptide made by the body. Researchers found it in 2001 while searching for genes that protect nerve cells from damage linked to Alzheimer’s disease.

Its code sits in the DNA of mitochondria, inside the gene for 16S ribosomal RNA. It was the first known “mitochondrial-derived peptide”, a group that now includes MOTS-c. A lab-made variant, HNG, is a more potent analog.

src.label: Yen et al., Aging (Albany NY), 2020 (full text, PMC)

what.text: How it acts, according to animal and cell studies:

items.text: In nerve cells in the lab, it blocked cell death caused by Alzheimer’s disease genes and beta-amyloid.
In rodents, humanin infused into the brain improved insulin sensitivity, and a potent humanin analog lowered blood sugar in diabetic rats.
In worms, extra humanin lengthened life slightly (19.0 against 17.7 days on average).

src.label: Yen et al., Aging (Albany NY), 2020 (full text, PMC)

what.text: None of these effects has been tested by giving humanin to people.

research.text: Human evidence: observational only. Studies measure humanin in blood or muscle and compare groups. No published human studies were found in which humanin itself was given to people, and no such trial is registered.
No published human studies found as of November 1, 2026 in which humanin was given to people. Seven registered studies mention humanin; all measure it rather than give it.

research.title: Humanin in children of centenarians

facts.v: Yen K, et al. Aging (Albany NY) 2020;12(12):11185-99
comparison of blood levels; no one was given humanin
18 children of people who lived to 100, and 19 controls of similar age

research.found: Children of centenarians had higher humanin than controls. The same paper reports lower humanin in Alzheimer’s disease and MELAS. Two authors are consultants and stockholders of CohBar Inc.

src.label: Yen et al., Aging (Albany NY), 2020 (full text, PMC)

research.title: Humanin with age and disease

facts.v: comparison of blood levels in healthy people of different ages and in patients
humanin, FGF21 and GDF15 in healthy people, type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s disease

research.found: Humanin rose with age in healthy people. It was lower in Alzheimer’s disease but not in type 2 diabetes. This differs from a 2009 study that found lower humanin in older people.

research.title: A humanin gene variant and cognitive ageing

facts.v: Yen K, et al. Sci Rep 2018;8(1):14212
genetic analysis in two human groups, plus mouse experiments
a variant (rs2854128) in the humanin code, blood humanin, cognitive tests in older adults

research.found: The variant was linked with lower blood humanin and, in a national sample of older adults, faster cognitive ageing. Two authors have consulted for CohBar Inc.

research.title: Humanin in muscle after strength training

facts.v: Gidlund EK, et al. Physiol Rep 2016;4(23):e13063
randomized to resistance training, Nordic walking or control; no one was given humanin
humanin in thigh muscle and blood

research.found: Muscle humanin rose 35% after resistance training. Blood humanin did not change in any group.

items.text: 18-month-old female mice given HNG (4 mg/kg into the belly twice a week) had less visceral fat, more lean mass and lower IGF-I. Lifespan did not differ at this dose.

src.label: Yen et al., Aging (Albany NY), 2020 (full text, PMC)

items.text: humanin given to old mice improved cognition.
worms with extra humanin lived slightly longer, depending on the daf-16/FOXO gene.

us.text: Not FDA-approved for any use. No humanin product appears in FDA’s drug approval database. Products labelled “research use only” are not for human use. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: none. A search of Drugs@FDA for humanin found no match.

FDA says products marketed “for research use only” or otherwise not for human consumption “have not been evaluated for safety and should never be used by humans.” Such products may not be sold for human use: FDA says it acts against firms selling unapproved products.

after.text: Humanin is not named on the WADA Prohibited List for 2026 or 2027. WADA’s class S0 bans at all times any pharmacological substance not covered elsewhere on the List and with no current approval by any government health regulator for human use. For 2027, WADA adds “peptides” to the examples in S0. The lists do not say whether humanin falls under S0.
Australia: Humanin is not named in the Poisons Standard that took effect on October 1, 2026. The TGA’s product register was not checked.

surprises: Humanin is promoted as a longevity peptide, but no published study has given it to a person; the human evidence is blood levels in small groups.
Studies disagree on whether humanin falls with age: a 2009 study found lower levels in older people, while a 2021 study found levels rose with age in healthy people.
In the 2020 study that treated middle-aged mice with the analog HNG, lifespan did not change at the dose tested.
